profiles.name: J. B. Childs
profiles.query: "J. B. Childs" IWW San Quentin 1923 portrait photograph
profiles.identity_context: J. B. Childs was from Los Angeles. J. B. Childs received a four-year prison sentence, which he served in San Quentin from July 12, 1923, until his term expired. Four months into his term at San Quentin, on November 16, Childs was beaten by a guard so severely that his head required four stitches; both his arms were "discolored, " and one of them bore a "deep cut." To protest the guard's brutality toward Childs, seventy-one IWW prisoners launched a work strike. They were all subsequently put "in solitary confinement on bread and water."
profiles.finding: Contemporary November1923 report corroborates San Quentin71-prisoner protest over beating; no identified sitter image found.

profiles.name: J. C. Robinson

profiles.identity_context: J. C. Robinson was a Los Angeles member of the Industrial Workers of the World, prosecuted under California's Criminal Syndicalism Act during the state's campaign to break IWW organizing. He and several co-defendants were convicted on July 11, 1923, and he was held at San Quentin as prisoner 38127. The Industrial Worker of August 6, 1924 lists him among the imprisoned and gives his birthday as August 19; no birth year is recorded. An appellate court afterwards reversed his conviction, and by March 4, 1925 he had been ordered released. The day he was arrested, the day he entered San Quentin and the day he actually walked out are all unresolved, so no time-served figure is published for him.

profiles.name: James P. Gordon

profiles.identity_context:
James P. Gordon was from Los Angeles. James P. Gordon received a five-year prison sentence, which he served in Folsom from July 12, 1923, until his term expired.

P. J. Gordon was imprisoned at Folsom State Prison during the era of California's criminal-syndicalism prosecutions, which sent more than a hundred IWW members and labor radicals to San Quentin and Folsom on one-to-fourteen-year terms. He appears on the International Labor Defense's rosters of American class-war prisoners in Labor Defender (1926-27); like most of the rank-and-file labor prisoners of the period, little else about his case entered the historical record.

The contemporary prisoner birthday list gives his birthday as February 13 (no birth year has surfaced). His prisoner number was 38113 — the 88113 rendered by the optical scan of the list was an error. Sentenced to five years under the California criminal-syndicalism campaign, he entered Folsom on July 12, 1923 and apparently remained until his term expired.
profiles.finding: Identity-specific search completed against prison, affiliation and date context. No adequately identified usable real portrait verified; source results indexed by query group. Archive research remains unresolved.

profiles.name: Josef Brencich
profiles.query: "Josef Brencich" Philadelphia deportation 1921 portrait photograph
profiles.identity_context: Josef Brencich was born in 1887 in Fiume, then part of Austria-Hungary, and immigrated to the United States in 1911. A sailor and painter, he was an Italian-speaking worker of Slavic background and belonged to the IWW-affiliated Union of Italian Workers. Federal authorities arrested him in Philadelphia in 1921 with Erasmo Abate and other union members and detained him during deportation proceedings. Officials initially ordered him deported to Hungary, then allowed voluntary departure on January 8, 1923 because Fiume had become an independent state. The exact arrest day has not been located.
profiles.finding: Philadelphia1921 deportation identity-specific search found no verified actual portrait; do not infer from other deportees.

profiles.name: William Burns
profiles.query: "William Burns" Yosemite IWW Leavenworth portrait photograph
profiles.identity_context: William Burns was arrested in Yosemite National Park for violating the California criminal syndicalism law by organizing for the IWW and "knowingly" becoming a member of the union. He was arrested in April 1923 and served approximately seventeen months in the county jail while awaiting trial. Because he was arrested in a federal park, Burns was tried in federal court. His jury consisted of a bank president, a "real estate shark, " a deputy sheriff, the superintendent of a bonding company and other persons with admitted prejudice against the IWW. Burns received a fifteen-month prison sentence, which he served in Leavenworth Penitentiary from November 1927 until May 14, 1928, when his sentence was commuted by President Calvin Coolidge.
profiles.finding: Yosemite IWW organizer corroborated contemporary1928 release reporting; modern Bill Burns2005 portrait, Florida military William Burns and FBI fugitive Elmer William Burns are unsupported identities; rejected.
